title: Infection Control, Safety & Hard Moments
summary: How not to carry an infection from one patient to the next, how not to get hurt, how the department catches errors before they reach a patient, and how to handle restraint, violence, fire, and death without falling apart.

lessons.title: Standard precautions and hand hygiene
lessons.body:
## Treat everything as infectious

**Standard precautions** are the baseline applied to every patient, every time, regardless of diagnosis. The reasoning is simple: you do not know who is infected. Half the people carrying a resistant organism have no idea, and the test result that would tell you arrives after you have already touched them.

So you treat blood, all body fluids except sweat, non-intact skin, and mucous membranes as infectious on every patient in the building.

Standard precautions include hand hygiene, gloves and gowns and eye protection matched to the expected exposure, respiratory etiquette, safe injection practice, safe sharps handling, and environmental cleaning.

## The five moments for hand hygiene

The World Health Organization framework is five moments, and it is worth memorizing because it answers "when" rather than leaving it to instinct.

1. **Before touching a patient.**
2. **Before a clean or aseptic procedure**, such as drawing blood cultures or handling an IV site.
3. **After body fluid exposure risk**, including immediately after removing gloves.
4. **After touching a patient.**
5. **After touching the patient's surroundings**, even if you never touched the patient. The bed rail is the patient.

> **Key:** Moment 5 is the one people skip. You adjusted a monitor cable, touched nothing else, and left. Your hands are contaminated.

## Alcohol rub or soap and water

Alcohol-based hand rub is preferred for most situations. It works faster, kills more organisms, and is gentler on skin than repeated washing. Use enough to keep hands wet for `20 to 30 seconds`, covering all surfaces including thumbs, fingertips, and between fingers, and rub until dry. Do not wipe it off.

**Soap and water is required when:**

- Hands are visibly soiled or feel sticky.
- You cared for a patient with **Clostridioides difficile** (C. diff).
- You cared for a patient with **norovirus**.
- Exposure to **Bacillus anthracis** is suspected.
- After using the restroom.

The reason for the C. diff and norovirus exceptions is mechanical. Both form or behave like spores, and alcohol does not kill spores. Soap and water works by physically washing them off, so scrub for at least `20 seconds` and dry with a towel.

## Gloves

Gloves are not a replacement for hand hygiene. They leak, they tear, and hands get contaminated during removal. So you do hand hygiene **before putting them on and after taking them off**, every time.

- Change gloves between patients, always.
- Change gloves between a dirty site and a clean site on the **same** patient, for example after perineal care before touching an IV site.
- Never wash or disinfect gloves to reuse them. Alcohol degrades the material and creates holes you cannot see.
- Do not walk the hallway in gloves. Gloved hands on a door handle, a computer, and a phone is a contamination trail with your name on it.

## Nails, jewelry, and what you wear

Artificial nails, extenders, gels, and wraps are prohibited for staff with direct patient contact. They harbor organisms under and around them and are linked to documented outbreaks, particularly in newborn and intensive care units. Natural nails stay shorter than `1/4 inch`.

Rings with stones, long bracelets, and dangling lanyards collect organisms and get grabbed. Hair up. Watch off or above the wrist.

> **On shift:** Foam or wash on the way in and on the way out of every room, out loud and visibly. Patients and families watch this, and so do your coworkers. It is the single most effective infection control measure that exists and it takes fifteen seconds.
keyPoints: Standard precautions apply to every patient, treating blood, all body fluids except sweat, non-intact skin, and mucous membranes as infectious.
The WHO five moments: before touching a patient, before an aseptic task, after fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, after touching their surroundings.
Alcohol rub for 20 to 30 seconds is preferred, but C. diff, norovirus, visible soiling, and restroom use require soap and water because alcohol does not kill spores.
Hand hygiene before gloves and after gloves, every time; never wash gloves for reuse.
No artificial nails for staff with patient contact; natural nails stay under 1/4 inch.

checks.q: You have just removed gloves after caring for a patient with C. difficile. What do you do?
choices: Alcohol rub, since your hands were gloved
Wash with soap and water, because alcohol does not kill C. diff spores
Nothing, because the gloves protected you
Alcohol rub followed by a second pair of gloves
checks.why: C. diff forms spores that alcohol cannot kill. Soap and water physically removes them. Gloves leak and hands get contaminated during removal, so gloving is never a substitute for hand hygiene.

checks.q: You entered a room only to silence an IV pump alarm and never touched the patient. What is required on the way out?
choices: Nothing, since there was no patient contact
Hand hygiene only if the patient is on precautions
Hand hygiene, because touching the patient's surroundings is moment 5
A gown change
checks.why: The patient's environment carries their organisms, and moment 5 exists for exactly this. Precaution status does not change the rule; standard precautions apply to everyone.

checks.q: You just finished perineal care on a patient and now need to draw blood from the same patient's arm. What is required?
choices: Continue with the same gloves since it is the same patient
Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, and put on new gloves before the clean task
Wipe the gloves with alcohol and continue
Put a second pair of gloves over the first
checks.why: Gloves are changed between a dirty site and a clean site on the same patient. Alcohol degrades glove material and creates invisible holes, and double gloving traps the contamination rather than removing it.

lessons.title: Transmission-based precautions and the sign on the door
lessons.body:
## Match the barrier to the route

When an organism spreads by a specific route, standard precautions are not enough and you add **transmission-based precautions**. There are three main categories plus a special-pathogen tier, and the category tells you exactly what to wear.

## Contact precautions

**Spread by touching the patient or their environment.**

Organisms: MRSA, VRE, C. difficile, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase and carbapenem-resistant organisms, scabies and lice, norovirus, RSV in children, draining wounds, and uncontained diarrhea or incontinence in an unknown situation.

Wear a **gown and gloves** for any entry into the room, not only for patient contact. Use dedicated equipment such as a stethoscope and blood pressure cuff left in the room, or disinfect shared equipment before it leaves.

**C. diff gets an enhanced version:** gowns and gloves, soap and water rather than alcohol, and bleach-based disinfectant for the room.

## Droplet precautions

**Spread by large respiratory droplets that travel a short distance, roughly `3 to 6 feet`, and fall.**

Organisms: influenza, pertussis (whooping cough), *Neisseria meningitidis* (meningococcus), mumps, rubella, group A streptococcus in the first `24 hours` of treatment, and adenovirus.

Wear a **surgical mask** plus eye protection when within a few feet. Private room preferred, door may stay open. **Put a surgical mask on the patient** any time they leave the room.

## Airborne precautions

**Spread by tiny particles that stay suspended and travel on air currents across a room and through a doorway.**

Organisms: tuberculosis, measles (rubeola), varicella (chickenpox), and disseminated herpes zoster (shingles).

Requirements are strict and non-negotiable:

- A **fit-tested N95 respirator** or a powered air-purifying respirator. A surgical mask does nothing here.
- An **airborne infection isolation room**, meaning negative pressure with `6 to 12` air changes per hour, exhausted outside or through a filter.
- **The door stays closed.** An open negative-pressure room is just a room.
- Mask the patient with a surgical mask, not an N95, for any transport, and transport only when necessary.

COVID-19 precautions vary by institution and by the current phase; follow your hospital's posted policy rather than what you remember from a previous year.

## Special pathogens

**Ebola and other viral hemorrhagic fevers** trigger a dedicated hospital protocol: a trained team, full coverage PPE with no exposed skin, and a **trained observer** who watches every step of donning and doffing. You do not improvise this.

**Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease** involves prions, which survive standard sterilization. It requires standard precautions plus special handling and disposal of instruments contacting brain tissue, spinal fluid, or the eye.

## Reading the sign

Every precaution room has a sign at the door listing exactly what to wear. Read it before you enter, not after. The signs are standardized within a hospital and color-coded, but the colors differ between hospitals, so read the words.

> **Trap:** The most common precaution failure is walking into a contact room to "just ask a question" without gowning. If you cross the threshold, you gown.

## Turning the room over

Cleaning is the last link in the chain and the tech is often doing it under flow pressure.

- Use an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant and respect the **wet contact time** on the label, usually `1 to 10 minutes`. The surface must stay visibly wet that entire time, or it is not disinfected. Wiping and walking away is theater.
- Clean **top to bottom and clean to dirty**, and never dip a used wipe back into the container.
- Hit the **high-touch surfaces**: bed rails, tray table, call bell and cord, IV pole, bedside table, door handles, light switches, monitor, keyboard, and the chair the family sat in.
- **C. diff and norovirus require a sporicidal agent, meaning bleach.** Standard quaternary wipes do not kill spores.
- Precaution rooms get a terminal clean by environmental services, including curtain changes. Know what your role is and what is theirs.
keyPoints: Contact precautions need gown and gloves for any room entry; C. diff adds soap and water and bleach.
Droplet precautions need a surgical mask within 3 to 6 feet; mask the patient to leave the room.
Airborne precautions need a fit-tested N95, a negative-pressure room with 6 to 12 air changes per hour, and a closed door.
TB, measles, varicella, and disseminated zoster are the airborne diseases you will actually encounter.
Disinfectant must keep the surface visibly wet for the full contact time on the label, and only bleach kills C. diff spores.

checks.q: A patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is placed in a negative-pressure room. A colleague props the door open to hear the patient better. What is the problem?
choices: Nothing, as long as everyone wears an N95
The negative pressure only functions with the door closed, so the isolation is defeated
The patient will get cold
The room alarm will sound but isolation is maintained
checks.why: Negative pressure depends on a sealed room to pull air inward and exhaust it. An open door lets infectious aerosols into the corridor, exposing everyone outside who is not wearing an N95.

checks.q: You need to enter a contact precautions room to ask the patient one question and will not touch anything. What do you wear?
choices: Nothing extra, since there is no contact
Gloves only
A surgical mask
Gown and gloves, because contact precautions apply to room entry, not just patient contact
checks.why: The patient's environment is contaminated, so the requirement is based on entering the room. Skipping the gown for a quick question is the single most common precaution failure in practice.

checks.q: You wipe a bedside table with a disinfectant wipe whose label says a 3-minute contact time. The surface dries in 45 seconds. What is required?
choices: Nothing; a single pass is sufficient
Reapply so the surface stays visibly wet for the full 3 minutes
Follow with an alcohol wipe
Let it dry and then wipe again with water
checks.why: Disinfectants are only validated at their labeled wet contact time. A surface that dries early has not been disinfected, so you reapply until the full duration is met. Alcohol and water do not substitute.

lessons.title: PPE: the order matters
lessons.body:
## Why there is an order at all

Personal protective equipment fails in a specific way: the outside of the gear becomes contaminated, and you contaminate yourself while taking it off. Every rule about sequence exists to solve that one problem.

The principle in one line: **put on in the order that lets each piece overlap the one before, and take off in the order that removes the dirtiest item first while it is still covering you.**

## Donning, in order

1. **Hand hygiene.**
2. **Gown.** Ties at the neck and waist, fully covering the torso from neck to knees and arms to the wrist, wrapping around the back.
3. **Mask or respirator.** Secure ties or elastic bands, fit the flexible band to the nose bridge, cover nose and mouth to under the chin. For an N95, **perform a seal check**: cover the respirator and exhale, and feel for leaks around the edges.
4. **Eye protection.** Goggles or a face shield, placed over the face and adjusted.
5. **Gloves.** Last, pulled **over the cuff of the gown** so no wrist skin is exposed.

Gown, mask, eyes, gloves. The gloves go on last because they seal the gown's weakest point.

## Doffing, in order

The outside of the gloves and the front of the gown are the dirtiest things in the room. The mask is the cleanest, because nothing should have touched it.

1. **Gloves.** Grasp the outside of one cuff and peel it off inside out, hold it in the gloved hand, slide a bare finger **under** the remaining cuff, and peel that one off over the first. Discard.
2. **Gown.** Untie or break the ties, pull away from the neck and shoulders touching only the inside, turn it inside out, and roll it into a bundle.
3. **Hand hygiene.**
4. **Eye protection.** Handle by the headband or earpieces only, never the front.
5. **Mask or respirator.** By the ties or elastic only, bottom first, then top, and lean forward as you lift it away from your face. Never touch the front.
6. **Hand hygiene again.**

> **Key:** Gloves and gown come off inside the room. Eye protection and the respirator come off at the doorway or after you step out, depending on policy, because the respirator is the last thing protecting you from the room's air.

## Sequence variations, and why they exist

Some facilities teach removing the gown and gloves together as one motion, rolling them off simultaneously into a bundle. Some doff eye protection before the gown. Follow your hospital's posted sequence, since they are all built on the same logic and consistency within a team matters more than a preferred variant.

For special pathogens such as Ebola, the sequence is longer, includes disinfecting gloved hands between steps, and requires a trained observer reading the steps aloud.

## N95 fit testing

An N95 works by sealing to your face. A leak of a few percent makes it a surgical mask with extra effort.

- Fit testing is done on hire and repeated at least annually, or whenever your face changes: significant weight change, dental surgery, facial scarring.
- The test is model and size specific. A fit test on one brand does not certify you for another.
- **Facial hair that crosses the seal breaks it.** A beard means a powered air-purifying respirator instead.
- Perform a **seal check every single time** you put one on. Fit testing was a one-time verification; the seal check is the per-use one.

> **Trap:** The most common contamination event is touching your own face or phone while still gloved. Once gloves are on, your hands belong to the patient, not to you.
keyPoints: Donning order: hand hygiene, gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, gloves over the gown cuff.
Doffing order: gloves, gown, hand hygiene, eye protection, mask, hand hygiene.
The order exists because the outside of gloves and the front of the gown are the most contaminated surfaces.
Gloves and gown come off inside the room; the respirator comes off last, at or outside the doorway.
N95s require annual fit testing by model and size, a seal check every use, and no facial hair crossing the seal.

checks.q: What is the correct doffing sequence?
choices: Gloves, gown, hand hygiene, eye protection, mask, hand hygiene
Mask, gloves, gown, eye protection, hand hygiene
Gown, gloves, mask, eye protection, hand hygiene
Eye protection, mask, gloves, gown, hand hygiene
checks.why: The most contaminated items come off first while still covered, and the respirator comes off last because it protects you from the room's air until you leave. Removing a mask early exposes your airway inside a contaminated room.

checks.q: Why do gloves go on last during donning?
choices: They are the cheapest item
They tear if worn too long
They cover the gown's cuff, sealing the exposed wrist
They interfere with tying the gown
checks.why: The wrist gap between glove and sleeve is the gown's weakest point, so gloves go over the cuff to close it. The gown's ties are a practical consideration, not the safety rationale.

checks.q: You were fit tested for a size medium N95 of one brand last year. Today only a different brand is stocked. What applies?
choices: Your fit test covers any N95 of the same size
Fit testing is model and size specific, so you need a fit test for this model or a different respirator
A seal check alone substitutes for fit testing
Any N95 is acceptable if you tighten the straps
checks.why: Respirator shapes differ by manufacturer, so a fit test certifies you for that specific model and size. A seal check is the per-use verification and does not replace formal fit testing.

lessons.title: Sharps, needlesticks, and what happens after
lessons.body:
## The rules that prevent it

OSHA's **Bloodborne Pathogens Standard**, 29 CFR 1910.1030, is the federal rule that governs this. It requires your employer to have a written exposure control plan, to provide hepatitis B vaccination at no cost to you, to use engineering controls such as safety-engineered needles and sharps containers, and to keep a sharps injury log.

The practical rules:

- **Never recap a needle.** Recapping causes a large share of all needlesticks. Activate the safety device immediately at the point of use, with one hand, while the needle is still under your control.
- **You dispose of your own sharp.** Not the nurse, not the next person. The person who used it walks it to the container.
- A sharps container gets replaced at about **three-quarters full**. Never press anything down into it, never reach in, never force a device past the opening.
- Bring the container to the sharp when possible, rather than carrying an exposed needle across the room.
- Do not hand a sharp directly to another person. Use a neutral zone, a tray or a flat surface, and announce it.
- Never leave a sharp on a bed, a sheet, a tray table, or in a pocket. A needle in linen is how a laundry worker gets stuck.

## The instant it happens

**1. Wash immediately.** Soap and water on the wound for at least `15 seconds`. Do **not** squeeze, do not milk the wound, and do not apply bleach or caustics. Squeezing and chemicals damage tissue and have never been shown to reduce transmission. For a splash to the eyes, nose, or mouth, flush with water or saline for `15 minutes` at an eyewash station.

**2. Report immediately.** To your charge nurse and to employee health or, after hours, through the ED itself. This is time-critical, not a paperwork step at end of shift.

**3. Source patient testing.** The source is tested for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C, following the consent rules in your state. Rapid HIV testing means an answer in minutes, which often makes prophylaxis unnecessary.

**4. Your baseline labs.** Drawn on you at the time of exposure.

## Post-exposure prophylaxis

**HIV.** If indicated, start post-exposure prophylaxis **as soon as possible, ideally within `2 hours`**, and no later than `72 hours` after exposure. The regimen runs `28 days`. Efficacy falls with every hour of delay, which is the entire reason for reporting immediately instead of finishing your shift.

**Hepatitis B.** If you completed the vaccine series and have documented immunity, no action is usually needed. If you are unvaccinated or a non-responder, hepatitis B immune globulin plus vaccine is given, ideally within `24 hours` and generally within `7 days`.

**Hepatitis C.** There is no prophylaxis and no vaccine. The approach is monitoring: testing at baseline and follow-up, with early antiviral treatment if you seroconvert. Cure rates with modern antivirals are very high, which is why follow-up testing actually matters.

**Follow-up schedule** is typically baseline, `6 weeks`, `12 weeks`, and `6 months`, shortened when newer combination assays are used. Complete it, even when you feel fine.

> **Key:** The clock is the whole thing. A needlestick reported at the end of a 12-hour shift may have crossed the window where prophylaxis works. Report it the minute it happens, every time, including for a patient you are sure is low risk.

## Staying protected in advance

- **Hepatitis B vaccine series** with a post-vaccination titer, free to you by law.
- **Annual influenza vaccine**, required by most hospitals.
- Documented immunity to measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella.
- **Tdap** once, then tetanus boosters.
- **TB screening** at hire, using a two-step skin test or an interferon gamma release assay blood test. Since 2019, CDC no longer recommends routine annual TB testing for health care personnel without a known exposure or ongoing risk, though many employers still require it.

> **On shift:** Know where the eyewash station is before you need it. You will not be reading signs with a chemical or blood splash in your eye.
keyPoints: Never recap needles; activate the safety device one-handed at the point of use and dispose of your own sharp.
Replace sharps containers at about three-quarters full and never push contents down or reach in.
After a stick: wash with soap and water 15 seconds without squeezing, flush mucous membranes 15 minutes, and report immediately.
HIV prophylaxis ideally within 2 hours and no later than 72 hours, for a 28-day course; hepatitis B immune globulin and vaccine within 24 hours if not immune.
There is no hepatitis C prophylaxis, so the follow-up testing schedule at baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, and 6 months is the protection.

checks.q: You sustain a needlestick from a used blood-draw needle at 0900. The patient appears healthy and low risk. What do you do?
choices: Report at the end of your shift since the risk is low
Wash, squeeze the wound to express blood, and report
Wash with soap and water without squeezing, and report immediately
Apply bleach to the wound and continue working
checks.why: Milking the wound and applying caustics damage tissue without reducing transmission. Reporting immediately matters because HIV prophylaxis is most effective within 2 hours, and apparent low risk is not a reason to delay.

checks.q: What is the outer time limit for starting HIV post-exposure prophylaxis?
choices: 2 hours
24 hours
72 hours
7 days
checks.why: Seventy-two hours is the outer limit, with 2 hours the ideal target because efficacy declines with delay. Twenty-four hours and 7 days are the hepatitis B immune globulin figures, not the HIV window.

checks.q: A sharps container is full to the top and a needle is protruding from the opening. What is the correct action?
choices: Push the needle down with a pen and continue using the container
Leave it and use another container while reporting the full container for replacement
Remove the protruding needle and place it in a new container
Tape over the opening
checks.why: Containers are replaced at about three-quarters full. Pushing contents down or reaching in causes sticks, and taping over the opening leaves a hazard in place for the next person.

lessons.title: The systems that catch errors
lessons.body:
## Identify the patient, every single time

Use **two identifiers** before every task on every patient: full name and date of birth, checked against the armband and against the label or order. Never the room number, never "the guy in bed 4," never a patient confirming a name you say to them, because sick, deaf, and confused patients say yes to anything.

Ask open-ended: "Tell me your full name and date of birth." If the armband and the label disagree in any character, stop and resolve it before anything is drawn, given, or sent.

> **Key:** Two identifiers is the rule that catches the wrong-patient error, and the wrong-patient error is the one that ends with a transfusion reaction or an operation on the wrong person.

## Wristband colors

Many states have standardized these, including a New Jersey effort, but **colors still vary between hospitals**, so read the printed words.

| Color | Usual meaning |
|---|---|
| Red | Allergy |
| Yellow | Fall risk |
| Purple | Do not resuscitate |
| Pink | Restricted extremity, no blood draws or blood pressures on that limb |
| Green | Latex allergy |

A restricted extremity band means a dialysis fistula, a mastectomy with lymph node removal, a PICC line, or a limb injury. Using it can cost the patient a fistula or cause lymphedema.

## Falls

Falls are the most common harm event in a hospital and the ED is the highest-risk setting: unfamiliar room, dim lighting, medications, IV lines, and patients who are dizzy, intoxicated, or too proud to ask.

What prevents them:

- Bed in the **lowest position** and locked, call bell in reach, non-skid socks, clear path to the bathroom.
- Yellow band and signage, and a **bed or chair alarm** where indicated.
- **Proactive toileting rounds**, because most falls happen on the way to a bathroom.
- Never leave a confused, intoxicated, sedated, or unsteady patient alone on a stretcher, ever, not even briefly.
- Two side rails up is standard. **Four rails up is considered a restraint** in most policies and creates an entrapment hazard, since a patient can slide into the gaps between rail, mattress, and frame and be strangled.

## Time-outs

Before any invasive procedure, everyone stops and verbally confirms: correct patient, correct procedure, correct site and side, correct position, consent present, equipment and imaging available. Everyone participates, and anyone can stop it. If you are in the room, you are part of the time-out.

## Never events

The National Quality Forum's serious reportable events are errors that should never happen: surgery on the wrong site or wrong patient, a retained foreign object, an ABO-incompatible transfusion, a death or serious injury from a fall, a hospital-acquired stage 3 or 4 pressure ulcer, a death associated with restraint use, and a patient elopement resulting in death or serious injury. Several of them are directly in your lane.

## Incident reports

An incident report, sometimes called a safety event report, exists to find system flaws, not to punish individuals. File one for a fall, a medication error, a needlestick, an equipment failure, a specimen error, an assault, a near miss, or anything that made you say "that was close."

Two rules:

1. **The report is not part of the medical record.** Chart the clinical facts in the chart and never write "incident report filed" in a patient's chart.
2. **Near misses are worth reporting.** Something that almost reached a patient is free information about a flaw that will eventually reach one.

Health care increasingly uses a **just culture** model, which separates honest human error from at-risk behavior and from reckless disregard. Honest errors get system fixes, not discipline. Hiding an error is what gets punished.

## If you witness a medication error

Speak up before it reaches the patient if you can do so safely. "Hold on, is that the right patient?" is a sentence any nurse would rather hear than not.

If it has already happened, tell the nurse and the provider immediately. The patient's safety comes first, the report comes second, and blame comes nowhere. Do not confront anyone in front of the patient, and do not decide on your own that it was probably fine.

> **On shift:** Speaking up about a colleague's error is the hardest professional skill in this job. Use a neutral, curious phrase rather than an accusation: "Can I check something with you?" It works, and it preserves the relationship you need for the next twelve hours.
keyPoints: Two identifiers, full name and date of birth, checked against the armband and label before every task.
Wristband colors vary by hospital, so read the words; a restricted extremity band protects fistulas, PICCs, and post-mastectomy limbs.
Falls are the most common hospital harm; bed low and locked, call bell in reach, proactive toileting, and never leave an unsteady patient alone on a stretcher.
Four side rails up is a restraint and an entrapment hazard; two is standard.
Incident reports stay out of the medical record, cover near misses, and exist for system learning under a just culture model.

checks.q: You approach a patient and say, 'Are you Robert Chen?' He nods. Is that acceptable identification?
choices: Yes, since he confirmed his name
No; ask him to state his full name and date of birth, and verify against the armband
Yes, if the room number also matches
Only if a family member is present to confirm
checks.why: Patients who are ill, hard of hearing, or confused agree to names that are not theirs. Open-ended identification plus armband verification is the standard, and room number is never an identifier.

checks.q: A patient has a pink restricted extremity band on the left arm. What does it prohibit?
choices: Ambulation without assistance
Any use of restraints
Blood draws, IVs, and blood pressures on that arm
Oral intake
checks.why: Restricted extremity typically means a dialysis fistula, a PICC, or a post-mastectomy limb, and using it risks destroying the fistula or causing lymphedema. Fall risk, restraints, and NPO status are indicated separately.

checks.q: You raise all four side rails on a confused patient's stretcher to keep him from getting up. What is wrong with this?
choices: Nothing; it is a standard fall precaution
Four rails up is considered a restraint in most policies and creates an entrapment and strangulation hazard
It is fine if the bed alarm is also on
It is only a problem for pediatric patients
checks.why: Full rails confine the patient, which meets the definition of a restraint requiring an order and monitoring, and patients have been strangled in the gaps between rail, mattress, and frame. Two rails plus a bed alarm and frequent checks is the standard approach.

lessons.title: Moving people without hurting them or yourself
lessons.body:
## Your back is career-limiting equipment

Health care has one of the highest rates of musculoskeletal injury of any industry, and the injuries come from patient handling. NIOSH research puts the maximum safe manual lift for patient handling at roughly **`35 pounds`** under ideal conditions. A human being is not 35 pounds, so the answer is almost always equipment and help, not technique.

The rule that keeps you working in ten years: **if you are wondering whether you need help, you need help.**

## The equipment

- **Friction-reducing slide sheets** for moving a patient up in bed or laterally. They cut the force required dramatically and are usually within arm's reach.
- **Air-assisted lateral transfer mats** for bed-to-stretcher moves of heavy or unstable patients.
- **Mechanical and ceiling lifts** for a patient who cannot bear weight.
- **Sit-to-stand devices** for patients with partial weight-bearing ability.
- **Gait belts** for ambulating, applied snugly around the waist over clothing. Hold the belt, never the patient's arm, never their clothing, never under the armpits.
- **Bariatric equipment.** Beds, stretchers, wheelchairs, and commodes each have a stated weight capacity printed on them. Check the number before you use it; standard equipment failing under load injures the patient and you.

## Technique that still matters

Feet apart for a wide base, bend at the knees and hips rather than the waist, load close to your body, **never twist** while loaded, pivot with your feet instead. Look where you are going. One person counts, out loud, "ready, set, move" so everyone moves together.

**Never lift alone over a threshold**: a doorway lip, an elevator gap, a curb, a ramp. That is where loads shift and backs go.

## Special precautions

**Hip precautions** after a posterior hip replacement: no bending the hip past `90 degrees`, no crossing the leg past midline, no rolling the leg inward. Use an elevated toilet seat and an abduction pillow, and do not let the patient bend forward to reach their feet.

**Spine precautions** for known or suspected spinal injury: maintain the head, neck, and trunk in alignment as one unit. A **log roll** takes three or four people: one at the head controlling the cervical spine who directs the whole move and calls the count, and two or three along the body turning together. Nobody moves until the head person says so.

## Transfers

Lock every wheel. Match bed and stretcher heights and lower the rails on the moving side. Transfer toward the patient's stronger side when they are assisting. For a bed to wheelchair transfer, place the chair at a slight angle on the stronger side, lock it, swing the footrests out of the way, gait belt on, and let the patient do everything they safely can.

## Transporting a patient out of the department

What you bring depends on the patient, and forgetting one item is how a routine trip to CT becomes an emergency in a hallway.

- **Monitor** if ordered, or if the patient is on continuous monitoring for any reason.
- **Oxygen**, with enough for the entire round trip plus reserve. Calculate it, do not guess.
- **IV pumps** with a charged battery, and enough fluid in the bag.
- **Chart, labels, and the patient's armband.**
- **Suction and an airway kit** for anyone with a compromised airway, active vomiting, or altered mental status.
- Emesis bag, blanket, and the call bell reminder for the patient.

### The oxygen duration formula

Duration in minutes equals tank pressure in psi minus a `200 psi` safe residual, times the tank constant, divided by the flow rate in liters per minute.

Tank constants: **D = `0.16`, E = `0.28`, M = `1.56`, H or K = `3.14`.**

Example: an E cylinder reading `2000 psi` running at `6 L/min`. That is `2000` minus `200` equals `1800`, times `0.28` equals `504`, divided by `6` equals **`84 minutes`**. Plenty for a CT. The same tank at `15 L/min` gives `33 minutes`, which is not.

## Handoff and the hallway

Give a verbal handoff at imaging: name and date of birth, why they are here, allergies, precautions, fall risk, code status, lines and drips, and who to call. **Never leave an unstable patient**, and never leave any patient unattended in a hallway or in a scanner room where no one is assigned to them.

> **On shift:** In an elevator, pull the stretcher in so the patient's head goes in first and stand at the head facing the patient. If the car is crowded, ask people to take the next one. It is not rude; it is a patient on a stretcher looking at the ceiling and strangers.
keyPoints: The safe manual patient lift limit is about 35 pounds, so equipment and extra people are the default, not technique.
Use slide sheets, air-assisted mats, mechanical lifts, sit-to-stand devices, and gait belts held at the belt.
Posterior hip precautions: no flexion past 90 degrees, no adduction past midline, no internal rotation.
A log roll needs three or four people with the person at the head controlling alignment and calling the count.
Oxygen duration equals pressure minus 200 psi, times the tank constant, divided by flow rate; E cylinder constant is 0.28.

checks.q: An E cylinder reads 1200 psi and the patient needs 4 L/min for a trip to CT and back, estimated at 40 minutes. Is the tank adequate?
choices: Yes; it provides about 70 minutes
No; it provides about 25 minutes
Yes, but only if the flow is reduced
Cannot be calculated without knowing the tank volume
checks.why: The calculation is 1200 minus 200, equals 1000, times 0.28 equals 280, divided by 4 equals 70 minutes, which comfortably covers a 40-minute trip. The constant for an E cylinder, 0.28, is what makes the calculation possible.

checks.q: A patient with a suspected spinal injury needs to be rolled to inspect his back. What is required?
choices: Two people, one at the shoulders and one at the hips
One person, rolling toward themselves slowly
A log roll with three or four people, the one at the head controlling alignment and calling the count
Raise the head of the bed first to make rolling easier
checks.why: The head, neck, and trunk must move as one unit, which needs a dedicated person at the head directing the move. Fewer people cannot maintain alignment, and raising the head of the bed flexes the spine, which is exactly what precautions prohibit.

checks.q: You are ambulating a weak patient with a gait belt and she begins to buckle. What do you do?
choices: Grab under her arms and lift her upright
Let go and call for help
Hold the gait belt, widen your stance, and lower her in a controlled way to the floor or a chair while calling for help
Pull her forward to regain momentum
checks.why: Attempting to hold up a falling adult injures both of you. A controlled lowering using the belt protects her head and your back. Lifting under the arms causes shoulder injury, and letting go produces an uncontrolled fall.

lessons.title: De-escalation, restraints, and seclusion
lessons.body:
## Least restrictive, always first

Restraint is a treatment failure that is sometimes necessary. Regulation, ethics, and outcome data all point the same way: everything less restrictive is tried first, and it is documented that it was tried.

## The de-escalation ladder

**1. Environment.** Lower the stimulation. Dim the lights, close the door, turn off the television, remove the audience. A crowd of six staff watching is fuel. Offer a quieter room.

**2. Basic needs.** An enormous number of escalations are hunger, cold, pain, nicotine withdrawal, a full bladder, or a phone with a dead battery. A sandwich, a blanket, a warm drink, or a phone call resolves more agitation than any medication.

**3. Verbal de-escalation.** Give them space, at least two arm lengths. Keep your hands visible and open, your posture at a slight angle rather than squared off, your voice lower and slower than theirs. Use their name. Listen and reflect: "You've been waiting four hours and nobody has told you anything. That would make me angry too." Offer real choices, because choice restores control: "Would you rather sit in the chair or on the bed?" Set limits plainly and without threat: "I want to help you. I can't do that if you're yelling at people."

**4. Show of presence.** Additional staff and security visible but not touching. Often ends it by itself.

**5. Voluntary medication**, offered by the nurse or provider, not by you.

**6. Physical restraint**, when the patient is an immediate danger to self or others and everything above has failed or is unsafe to attempt.

> **Key:** The single most effective de-escalation tool is telling an angry person something true about their situation and then doing one concrete thing for them.

## Two kinds of restraint order

**Medical or non-violent restraint** prevents interference with treatment, for example a delirious patient pulling out an endotracheal tube. Orders are renewed per hospital policy, typically each calendar day with a fresh assessment.

**Behavioral or violent restraint** manages violent or self-destructive behavior. Federal rules are strict:

- A **face-to-face evaluation** by a physician, licensed independent practitioner, or trained registered nurse or physician assistant is required **within `1 hour`** of initiation.
- Orders are time limited: **`4 hours` for adults 18 and over, `2 hours` for ages 9 to 17, `1 hour` for children under 9.** Renewal requires a new order.
- **No PRN and no standing orders.** Restraint cannot be ordered in advance or "as needed."

**Seclusion** is involuntary confinement alone in a room the patient cannot leave, and it is permitted only for violent or self-destructive behavior under the same rules.

## Applying and monitoring

The application itself is a team event with a designated leader who does the talking, one person per limb, and one person controlling the head. Someone keeps explaining what is happening the entire time.

- **Never prone with pressure on the back.** Positional asphyxia kills. Supine with the head of the bed slightly elevated is standard, with airway and vomiting risk watched continuously.
- **Never tie to the side rails.** Tie to the bed frame, on the part that moves with the bed, so a rail drop does not wrench a limb.
- **Quick-release knots only**, never a knot that needs scissors. You must be able to release every limb in seconds for vomiting, a code, or a fire.
- **Checks at least every `15 minutes`**, documenting circulation, skin integrity, range of motion of each limb, respiratory status and airway, position, and offers of **fluids, food, and toileting**. Release limbs one at a time for range of motion per policy.
- Continuous observation, usually a 1:1 sitter, for behavioral restraint.

**Chemical restraint** means medication given to control behavior rather than to treat a diagnosed condition. You never administer it, but you will be present: watch for oversedation, a falling respiratory rate, and airway compromise, and report any change immediately.

## The reason for the rules

People die in restraints. The documented mechanisms are positional asphyxia from prone restraint or weight on the chest, strangulation from a vest or an improperly tied limb, aspiration in a supine sedated patient, and cardiac events in agitated, intoxicated, or medically ill patients. A death associated with restraint use is a reportable never event.

> **Trap:** The most dangerous moment is not the application. It is the twenty minutes after, when the room is quiet, staff have dispersed, and everyone assumes someone else is watching.
keyPoints: Restraint is last: environment, basic needs, verbal de-escalation, show of presence, offered medication, then physical restraint.
Behavioral restraint requires a face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour and time-limited orders of 4 hours for adults, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, and 1 hour under age 9.
PRN and standing restraint orders are prohibited.
Never prone with pressure on the back, never tied to side rails, quick-release knots only.
Checks at least every 15 minutes covering circulation, skin, range of motion, breathing, position, and offers of fluids and toileting.

checks.q: A 34-year-old adult is placed in behavioral restraints at 1400. When must the order be renewed, and when is the face-to-face evaluation due?
choices: Renewed at 1600, face-to-face by 1500
Renewed at 1800, face-to-face by 1500
Renewed at 2200, face-to-face within 4 hours
No renewal needed for 24 hours
checks.why: Adult behavioral restraint orders are limited to 4 hours, so renewal is due at 1800, and a face-to-face evaluation is required within 1 hour of initiation. The 2-hour limit applies to ages 9 to 17.

checks.q: A restrained patient begins vomiting. What is the immediate priority?
choices: Call the provider for an order to release the restraints
Turn the patient's head, suction, and release restraints as needed using the quick-release knots while calling for help
Document the event and increase monitoring frequency
Place the patient prone so the vomit drains
checks.why: Aspiration is a leading cause of restraint-associated death, so airway protection comes first and quick-release knots exist for exactly this. Waiting for an order costs the airway, and prone positioning with restraint risks positional asphyxia.

checks.q: An agitated patient is pacing and shouting that no one has told him anything for three hours. What is the best first intervention?
choices: Call security to stand in the doorway
Tell him he needs to calm down or he will be restrained
Acknowledge the wait honestly, use his name, offer a chair and a drink, and commit to one concrete thing you will do
Leave the room until he calms down
checks.why: Verbal de-escalation with a true acknowledgment plus one concrete action resolves most agitation at this stage. Threats escalate, an immediate show of force skips the ladder, and leaving without a plan abandons the situation to worsen.

lessons.title: Violence, codes overhead, and fire
lessons.body:
## Emergency departments are the most violent place in the hospital

Health care workers absorb a large share of all workplace violence injuries in the United States, and the ED is the epicenter: intoxication, withdrawal, psychiatric crisis, pain, fear, long waits, and grief, all in one room.

## Reading escalation early

Violence has a runway. Watch for pacing, refusing to sit, clenched fists or jaw, rapid loud speech, invading personal space, staring or repeatedly scanning exits, escalating demands, throwing or slamming objects, sudden silence after agitation, and direct threats.

## Positioning that keeps you safe

- Keep **two arm lengths** of distance, more if possible.
- Stand at a slight angle, not squared off, with hands visible and open.
- **Keep a clear path to the door and never let the patient get between you and the exit.**
- **Never turn your back** on an escalating person.
- Remove anything that can be grabbed or used against you: dangling stethoscope, lanyard, necklaces, long hair down, badge on a breakaway clip.
- Do not enter a room alone with someone who is escalating. Bring a second person, and bring security early rather than late.
- Know where the **panic buttons** are, at the desk, in triage, and in safe rooms, and know the overhead code your hospital uses for a combative person and for a weapon.

**Report every incident.** Verbal threats included. Underreporting is the reason the problem stays invisible, and patterns identified in reports are what drive staffing and security changes. New Jersey has required violence prevention programs in health care facilities since the Violence Prevention in Health Care Facilities Act took effect, and New Jersey law treats assaulting a health care worker performing their duties as a more serious offense than simple assault. Your employer's security policy will name the exact process.

> **Key:** You are never obligated to stay in a room with someone who is threatening you. Leaving to get help is a professional action, not a failure.

## Codes overhead

These **vary between hospitals** and some systems have moved to plain language announcements. Learn your hospital's list in orientation; here are common conventions.

| Code | Common meaning |
|---|---|
| Blue | Cardiac or respiratory arrest |
| Stroke, STEMI, Sepsis | Time-critical treatment alerts |
| Trauma alert | Trauma team activation |
| Pink | Infant or child abduction |
| Silver | Person with a weapon or active shooter |
| Gray | Combative or aggressive person |
| Orange | Hazardous material spill |
| Red | Fire |
| Triage or Yellow | Mass casualty or external disaster |

For a **code pink**, every staff member becomes a set of eyes. Staff cover exits and stairwells and look for anyone carrying a bag, box, or bundle, or anyone leaving quickly.

For a **code silver**, the guidance is run, hide, fight, in that order, and you do not go looking.

## Fire: RACE and PASS

**RACE** is the sequence.

- **R: Rescue** anyone in immediate danger.
- **A: Alarm.** Pull the station and call the emergency number.
- **C: Contain.** Close doors and windows to starve the fire of air and slow smoke.
- **E: Extinguish or Evacuate.** Only fight a small, contained fire with a clear escape at your back.

**PASS** is how to use the extinguisher.

- **P: Pull** the pin.
- **A: Aim** at the **base** of the flames, not the flames themselves.
- **S: Squeeze** the handle.
- **S: Sweep** side to side.

Evacuation is horizontal first, meaning through the nearest fire doors into the adjacent smoke compartment, then vertical by stairs. **Never use an elevator in a fire.**

## Oxygen and fire

Oxygen does not burn, but it makes everything else burn faster and hotter. In an oxygen-enriched space, a spark that would be harmless becomes a flash fire, and this is why surgical fires and home oxygen fires exist.

Zone valves in the hallway shut off piped oxygen to a section of the department. **Only shut them down on the order of the person running the response**, because closing a valve stops oxygen to every patient in that zone, including a patient on a ventilator.

> **On shift:** In your first week find the pull stations, the extinguishers, the oxygen zone valves, the fire doors, and the stairwells. Fire drills are boring until the one that is not a drill.
keyPoints: Escalation warning signs include pacing, clenched fists, rapid loud speech, invading space, scanning exits, and sudden silence.
Keep two arm lengths, stand at an angle, keep a clear exit, never turn your back, and remove grabbable items.
Report every violent incident including verbal threats; New Jersey requires health care violence prevention programs and treats assault on a health care worker as a heightened offense.
RACE is rescue, alarm, contain, extinguish or evacuate; PASS is pull, aim at the base, squeeze, sweep.
Oxygen accelerates combustion; shut zone valves only on the order of the person running the response.

checks.q: You discover a small fire in a linen cart in a hallway. A patient room is adjacent. What is the correct order of actions?
choices: Extinguish first, then alarm, then move the patient
Rescue anyone in immediate danger, pull the alarm, close doors to contain, then extinguish if it is small and you have an exit
Evacuate the entire department immediately by elevator
Shut the oxygen zone valve, then call for help
checks.why: RACE puts people first, then the alarm so help is coming, then containment, and only then extinguishing. Elevators are never used in a fire, and zone valves are shut only on command because they cut oxygen to every patient in the zone.

checks.q: A patient's demands are escalating and he steps between you and the door. What should you do?
choices: Continue talking calmly from where you are
Move so you have a clear path to the exit, keep distance, and call for help
Turn away and walk to the far corner to give him space
Reach past him for the door handle
checks.why: Losing your exit is the position that turns an escalation into an assault. Repositioning for an exit while maintaining distance and summoning help is correct. Moving to a corner traps you, and reaching past him invites contact.

checks.q: Where do you aim a fire extinguisher?
choices: At the top of the flames
At the middle of the flames
At the base of the flames
Above the flames so the agent falls down
checks.why: The base is where the fuel is burning, and cutting off the fuel source extinguishes the fire. Aiming at the visible flames wastes the agent on the part of the fire that is already burning off.

lessons.title: Death in the department
lessons.body:
## It happens, and there is a process

Death in the ED is sudden, public, and usually unexpected by the family. There is a defined sequence, and doing it correctly is one of the more meaningful things you will ever do.

A provider pronounces death and documents the time. Nothing about post-mortem care begins until that has happened and you know one thing: **is this a medical examiner case?**

## Medical examiner cases

In New Jersey, as in every state, certain deaths are reported to the medical examiner. The categories typically include deaths that are violent, meaning homicide, suicide, or accident, deaths that are sudden or unexpected in an apparently healthy person, deaths in custody, deaths from suspected overdose, occupational deaths, deaths related to a procedure, unattended deaths, and any death where the cause is unknown or suspicious. Most ED deaths qualify.

**In a medical examiner case, nothing is removed.** Not the endotracheal tube, not the IV lines, not the intraosseous needle, not the defibrillator pads, not the clothing, not dressings. Do not wash the body. Do not clean blood off. Everything on and around that body is potential evidence, and every tube's position may be a question later.

Save clothing rather than discarding it, in a paper bag if it is wet with blood. When in doubt, leave it and ask.

> **Key:** Assume every ED death is a medical examiner case until someone tells you it is not. Nothing removed, nothing cleaned, nothing discarded.

## Organ and tissue donation referral

Federal rules require hospitals to notify the local organ procurement organization of every death and every imminent death, usually within about `1 hour`. In New Jersey that is the NJ Sharing Network, and the referral is made whether or not anyone believes the patient is a candidate, because tissue and cornea donation remains possible after cardiac death.

**Staff do not approach the family about donation.** A trained requestor from the procurement organization does, because how the request is made measurably changes both consent rates and family distress. If a family raises it with you, say that a specialist will speak with them, and tell the nurse.

## Family presence during resuscitation

Professional guidance supports offering family the option to be present, with a staff member assigned to stay with them. Families who are present report less anxiety and less complicated grief than those left in a waiting room imagining it.

If you are that person, your job is narration and presence, not clinical detail. "They're doing chest compressions to keep blood moving. The doctor is putting a tube in to breathe for him." Then stand there, and do not fill the silence.

## What to say to a family

Sit down. Use the patient's name. Say **died** or **dead**, plainly and early. Softened words such as "passed," "lost," and "didn't make it" are routinely misunderstood by people in shock, who then ask when he is going upstairs.

What not to say: "I know how you feel," "at least he didn't suffer," "she's in a better place," or anything that begins with "at least."

What works: "I'm so sorry." Silence. Concrete offers: water, a chair, a private room, a phone, a chaplain. Answer the question asked, and say "I don't know, but I'll find out" when you do not.

## Viewing the body, and belongings

Make the room presentable within the limits of a medical examiner case: straighten the sheets, dim the lights, place a chair by the bed, remove trash. Tell them what they will see before they walk in, especially tubes, bruising from resuscitation, or facial injury. Offer to go in with them or wait outside, and honor whichever they choose. Do not rush this.

Inventory belongings with a second staff member as witness. Valuables go to the hospital safe with a receipt. Return everything in a proper belongings bag, never a trash bag. Clothing that was cut off is still theirs.

## Afterward, for you

The term for the clinician harmed by a bad outcome is the **second victim**, and it is real: intrusive replaying, self-doubt, anxiety, and avoidance, whether or not anything was done wrong.

Go to the debrief. Say the thing that bothered you out loud. Use peer support and the employee assistance program, and know that a delayed reaction, arriving three days or three weeks later, is normal.

> **On shift:** After a death the department keeps moving and someone has to turn the room over. Take the ninety seconds it costs to wash your hands slowly and breathe before the next room. That is how people last in this job.
keyPoints: Assume every ED death is a medical examiner case: remove no tubes or lines, do not wash the body, and preserve clothing and belongings.
Every death and imminent death is referred to the organ procurement organization, usually within about 1 hour, and staff never approach the family about donation themselves.
Family presence during resuscitation is supported when a staff member is assigned to stay with and narrate for them.
Say died or dead plainly; avoid softened language, 'at least' statements, and claims to know how they feel.
The second victim response is real and normal; use debriefs, peer support, and the employee assistance program.

checks.q: A patient dies after an unsuccessful resuscitation for a suspected overdose. What do you do with the endotracheal tube and IV lines?
choices: Remove them before the family views the body
Remove only the lines that are not bleeding
Leave everything in place, because this is a medical examiner case
Remove them and document their prior position
checks.why: Suspected overdose deaths are reportable to the medical examiner, and tube and line placement can be a forensic question. Nothing is removed, nothing is washed, and documentation does not substitute for preserving the body as it is.

checks.q: A grieving wife asks you whether her husband could be an organ donor. What is the correct response?
choices: Explain the donation process and ask whether she consents
Tell her it is too late once the heart has stopped
Say a specialist will speak with her about it, and notify the nurse
Tell her to call the donor registry herself
checks.why: Only a trained requestor from the organ procurement organization approaches families, because how the request is made changes both consent and family distress. Tissue and cornea donation remains possible after cardiac death, so the premise that it is too late is wrong.

checks.q: Which phrase is appropriate when telling a family about a death?
choices: 'He passed on to a better place'
'At least she didn't suffer'
'I know exactly how you feel'
'I'm so sorry. He died.'
checks.why: Plain words prevent the misunderstanding that people in shock routinely have with softened language. 'At least' statements minimize the loss, and claiming to know how someone feels centers you instead of them.

cards.front: What do standard precautions treat as infectious, and for whom?
cards.back: Blood, all body fluids except sweat, non-intact skin, and mucous membranes, on every patient regardless of diagnosis, because you cannot know who is colonized or infected.

cards.front: What are the WHO five moments for hand hygiene?
cards.back: Before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching the patient's surroundings.

cards.front: Which moment for hand hygiene is most often skipped?
cards.back: Moment 5, after touching the patient's surroundings. Adjusting a monitor or a bed rail and touching nothing else still contaminates your hands.

cards.front: When must you use soap and water instead of alcohol rub?
cards.back: Visibly soiled hands, C. difficile, norovirus, suspected Bacillus anthracis, and after using the restroom. Alcohol does not kill spores; soap and water physically removes them.

cards.front: How long should alcohol hand rub and soap-and-water washing each take?
cards.back: Alcohol rub: enough product to keep hands wet 20 to 30 seconds, rubbed until dry, never wiped off. Soap and water: scrub at least 20 seconds, then dry with a towel.

cards.front: Why are gloves not a substitute for hand hygiene?
cards.back: Gloves leak and tear, and hands get contaminated during removal. Perform hand hygiene before donning and after removing, every time, and never wash or disinfect gloves for reuse.

cards.front: When do you change gloves on the same patient?
cards.back: Moving from a dirty site to a clean site, such as after perineal care before touching an IV site. Also always between patients.

cards.front: What are the rules on nails for staff with patient contact?
cards.back: No artificial nails, extenders, gels, or wraps, because they harbor organisms and are linked to outbreaks in newborn and intensive care units. Natural nails stay under 1/4 inch.

cards.front: Which organisms require contact precautions?
cards.back: MRSA, VRE, C. difficile, ESBL and carbapenem-resistant organisms, scabies and lice, norovirus, RSV in children, and draining wounds. Gown and gloves for any room entry.

cards.front: Which organisms require droplet precautions and what do you wear?
cards.back: Influenza, pertussis, meningococcus, mumps, rubella, group A strep in the first 24 hours, adenovirus. Surgical mask plus eye protection within 3 to 6 feet; mask the patient to leave the room.

cards.front: Which diseases require airborne precautions?
cards.back: Tuberculosis, measles, varicella (chickenpox), and disseminated herpes zoster. Fit-tested N95 or PAPR, negative-pressure room with 6 to 12 air changes per hour, door closed.

cards.front: Why must an airborne isolation room door stay closed?
cards.back: Negative pressure only works with a sealed room. An open door lets infectious aerosols into the corridor, exposing everyone outside who is not wearing an N95.

cards.front: What mask goes on a TB patient being transported?
cards.back: A surgical mask on the patient, not an N95. The surgical mask contains what they exhale. Staff wear the N95. Transport only when necessary.

cards.front: What is different about C. diff precautions?
cards.back: Contact precautions plus soap and water instead of alcohol for hand hygiene, and a bleach-based sporicidal disinfectant for the room. Standard quaternary wipes do not kill spores.

cards.front: What is special about Ebola and other viral hemorrhagic fever precautions?
cards.back: A dedicated hospital protocol with a trained team, full coverage PPE with no exposed skin, and a trained observer who watches and reads aloud every step of donning and doffing. You never improvise it.

cards.front: Why does Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease need special handling?
cards.back: Prions survive standard sterilization. Standard precautions apply, plus special handling and disposal of instruments contacting brain tissue, spinal fluid, or the eye.

cards.front: What is 'wet contact time' and why does it matter?
cards.back: The time a disinfectant must keep a surface visibly wet to actually kill organisms, usually 1 to 10 minutes per the label. A surface that dries early has not been disinfected; reapply.

cards.front: Which are the high-touch surfaces in a room turnover?
cards.back: Bed rails, tray table, call bell and cord, IV pole, bedside table, door handles, light switches, monitor, keyboard, and the family chair. Clean top to bottom and clean to dirty.

cards.front: What is the PPE donning order?
cards.back: Hand hygiene, gown, mask or respirator with a seal check, eye protection, then gloves pulled over the gown cuff.

cards.front: What is the PPE doffing order?
cards.back: Gloves, gown, hand hygiene, eye protection, mask or respirator, hand hygiene again.

cards.front: Why does the doffing order start with gloves and end with the mask?
cards.back: Glove exteriors and the gown front are the most contaminated surfaces and come off while still covering you. The respirator is the last thing protecting you from the room's air, so it comes off last.

cards.front: How do you remove gloves without contaminating your hands?
cards.back: Grasp the outside of one cuff, peel it off inside out, hold it in the gloved hand, slide a bare finger under the other cuff, and peel that one off over the first.

cards.front: Which PPE comes off inside the room versus outside?
cards.back: Gloves and gown come off inside the room. Eye protection and the respirator come off at the doorway or after stepping out, per policy, because the respirator protects you from the room's air.

cards.front: What is the difference between N95 fit testing and a seal check?
cards.back: Fit testing is a formal annual verification specific to one model and size. A seal check is done every single time you put the respirator on: cover it, exhale, and feel for leaks around the edges.

cards.front: Why can a bearded staff member not wear an N95?
cards.back: An N95 works by sealing against skin, and facial hair crossing the seal breaks it. The alternative is a powered air-purifying respirator, which does not require a facial seal.

cards.front: What does OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard require of an employer?
cards.back: A written exposure control plan, free hepatitis B vaccination, engineering controls such as safety needles and sharps containers, work practice controls, PPE, and a sharps injury log.

cards.front: What are the core rules of sharps handling?
cards.back: Never recap, activate the safety device one-handed at the point of use, dispose of your own sharp, bring the container to the sharp, never hand a sharp person to person, never leave one in linen or on a bed.

cards.front: When is a sharps container replaced?
cards.back: At about three-quarters full. Never press contents down, never reach in, and never force a device past the opening.

cards.front: What do you do in the first minute after a needlestick?
cards.back: Wash the wound with soap and water for at least 15 seconds without squeezing or applying caustics, or flush a mucous membrane splash with water or saline for 15 minutes, then report immediately.

cards.front: Why is squeezing or bleaching a needlestick wound wrong?
cards.back: Neither has been shown to reduce transmission, and both damage tissue. The actions that matter are washing, immediate reporting, source testing, and timely prophylaxis.

cards.front: What is the time window for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis?
cards.back: Start as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours, and no later than 72 hours after exposure. The regimen runs 28 days and efficacy falls with every hour of delay.

cards.front: What happens for hepatitis B after an exposure?
cards.back: If you completed the vaccine series with documented immunity, usually nothing. If unvaccinated or a non-responder, hepatitis B immune globulin plus vaccine, ideally within 24 hours and generally within 7 days.

cards.front: What is the approach to hepatitis C after an exposure?
cards.back: There is no prophylaxis and no vaccine. Baseline and follow-up testing, with early antiviral treatment if you seroconvert. Modern antivirals cure the great majority of cases, which is why follow-up matters.

cards.front: What is the typical post-exposure follow-up testing schedule?
cards.back: Baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, and 6 months, shortened when newer combination assays are used. Complete it even when you feel fine.

cards.front: What vaccines and screenings does a health care worker need?
cards.back: Hepatitis B series with a titer, annual influenza, documented measles mumps rubella and varicella immunity, Tdap, and TB screening at hire by two-step skin test or interferon gamma release assay.

cards.front: What are the two patient identifiers and how do you ask for them?
cards.back: Full name and date of birth, checked against the armband and the label. Ask open-ended: 'tell me your full name and date of birth.' Never room number, never a name the patient only confirms.

cards.front: What do the common wristband colors mean?
cards.back: Red allergy, yellow fall risk, purple do not resuscitate, pink restricted extremity, green latex allergy. Colors vary by hospital, so always read the printed words.

cards.front: What does a restricted extremity band prohibit and why?
cards.back: No blood draws, IVs, or blood pressures on that limb. It marks a dialysis fistula, a PICC, a post-mastectomy arm, or an injury, and using it can destroy a fistula or cause lymphedema.

cards.front: What are the core fall precautions in an ED room?
cards.back: Bed lowest and locked, call bell in reach, non-skid socks, clear path to the bathroom, yellow band and signage, bed or chair alarm where indicated, and proactive toileting rounds.

cards.front: Why is raising all four side rails a problem?
cards.back: It meets the definition of a restraint in most policies and creates an entrapment hazard, since patients can slide into gaps between rail, mattress, and frame and be strangled. Two rails up is standard.

cards.front: What does a procedural time-out confirm?
cards.back: Correct patient, correct procedure, correct site and side, correct position, consent present, and equipment and imaging available. Everyone in the room participates and anyone can stop it.

cards.front: Name five never events relevant to an ED tech.
cards.back: Death or serious injury from a fall, a death associated with restraint use, an elopement resulting in death or serious injury, an ABO-incompatible transfusion, and a hospital-acquired stage 3 or 4 pressure ulcer.

cards.front: Two rules about incident reports?
cards.back: They are not part of the medical record, so never chart that one was filed. And near misses get reported too, because something that almost reached a patient reveals a flaw that eventually will.

cards.front: What does 'just culture' mean?
cards.back: A model separating honest human error from at-risk behavior and reckless disregard. Honest errors get system fixes rather than discipline. What gets punished is hiding an error.

cards.front: You see a nurse about to give a medication to what looks like the wrong patient. What do you say?
cards.back: Speak up before it reaches the patient, using a neutral phrase: 'Hold on, can I check something with you?' Patient safety first, report second, never a confrontation in front of the patient.

cards.front: What is the recommended maximum manual patient lift, and what follows from it?
cards.back: About 35 pounds under ideal conditions. Since no patient weighs that, equipment and additional people are the default rather than better technique.

cards.front: Name five pieces of safe patient handling equipment.
cards.back: Friction-reducing slide sheets, air-assisted lateral transfer mats, mechanical or ceiling lifts, sit-to-stand devices, gait belts, and rated bariatric beds, stretchers, and chairs.

cards.front: How is a gait belt used correctly?
cards.back: Snug around the waist over clothing, and you hold the belt. Never hold the patient's arm, clothing, or under the armpits, which causes shoulder injury and gives you no control.

cards.front: What are posterior hip precautions?
cards.back: No hip flexion past 90 degrees, no crossing the leg past midline, no inward rotation of the leg. Use an elevated toilet seat and an abduction pillow, and do not let them bend to reach their feet.

cards.front: How is a log roll performed?
cards.back: Three or four people moving the head, neck, and trunk as one unit. The person at the head controls cervical alignment, directs the move, and calls the count; nobody moves until they say so.

cards.front: What is the oxygen tank duration formula?
cards.back: Duration in minutes equals (tank pressure in psi minus 200 psi residual) times the tank constant, divided by flow rate in L/min. Constants: D = 0.16, E = 0.28, M = 1.56, H or K = 3.14.

cards.front: How long does an E cylinder at 2000 psi last at 6 L/min?
cards.back: About 84 minutes. (2000 minus 200) times 0.28 equals 504, divided by 6 equals 84. The same tank at 15 L/min lasts about 33 minutes.

cards.front: What do you bring on a patient transport out of the department?
cards.back: Monitor if ordered, oxygen with enough for the round trip plus reserve, IV pumps with charged batteries, chart and labels, suction and airway kit for anyone with airway risk, emesis bag and blanket.

cards.front: What goes into a handoff at imaging?
cards.back: Name and date of birth, why they are here, allergies, precautions, fall risk, code status, lines and drips, and who to call. Never leave an unstable patient or any unattended patient in a hallway.

cards.front: What are the six rungs of the de-escalation ladder?
cards.back: Reduce environmental stimulation, meet basic needs, verbal de-escalation, show of presence, voluntary medication offered by the nurse or provider, and only then physical restraint.

cards.front: What does effective verbal de-escalation sound like?
cards.back: Two arm lengths of space, hands visible, angled posture, voice lower and slower than theirs, their name used, honest acknowledgment of the problem, real choices offered, limits set without threats.

cards.front: What is the difference between medical and behavioral restraint orders?
cards.back: Medical restraint prevents interference with treatment and is renewed per policy, typically daily. Behavioral restraint manages violent or self-destructive behavior and carries strict federal time limits and a 1-hour face-to-face requirement.

cards.front: What are the behavioral restraint order time limits by age?
cards.back: 4 hours for adults 18 and over, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, 1 hour for children under 9. Renewal requires a new order, and PRN or standing restraint orders are prohibited.

cards.front: How soon must a face-to-face evaluation occur after behavioral restraint is initiated?
cards.back: Within 1 hour, by a physician, licensed independent practitioner, or a trained registered nurse or physician assistant, depending on hospital policy.

cards.front: What is checked every 15 minutes on a restrained patient?
cards.back: Circulation and pulses distal to the restraint, skin integrity, range of motion of each limb, respiratory status and airway, position, and offers of fluids, food, and toileting.

cards.front: What three positioning rules prevent restraint deaths?
cards.back: Never prone with pressure on the back, because of positional asphyxia. Never tie to side rails; tie to the bed frame that moves with the bed. Quick-release knots only, releasable in seconds.

cards.front: What is chemical restraint and what is your role?
cards.back: Medication given to control behavior rather than treat a diagnosed condition. You never administer it, but you monitor for oversedation, falling respiratory rate, and airway compromise and report changes immediately.

cards.front: How do people die in restraints?
cards.back: Positional asphyxia from prone restraint or chest pressure, strangulation from a vest or an improperly tied limb, aspiration in a sedated supine patient, and cardiac events in agitated or intoxicated patients.

cards.front: What are the warning signs that a person is about to become violent?
cards.back: Pacing, refusing to sit, clenched fists or jaw, rapid loud speech, invading personal space, scanning exits, escalating demands, throwing or slamming objects, sudden silence after agitation, and direct threats.

cards.front: How do you position yourself with an escalating patient?
cards.back: Two arm lengths of distance, angled stance with hands visible, a clear path to the door, never letting them between you and the exit, never turning your back, and nothing dangling to be grabbed.

cards.front: Why report verbal threats and not just physical assaults?
cards.back: Underreporting keeps the problem invisible. Patterns from reports drive staffing, security, and design changes. New Jersey requires violence prevention programs in health care facilities and treats assault on a health care worker as a heightened offense.

cards.front: What do these overhead codes commonly mean: blue, pink, silver, gray, orange, red?
cards.back: Blue is cardiac or respiratory arrest, pink is infant or child abduction, silver is a weapon or active shooter, gray is a combative person, orange is a hazardous material spill, red is fire. Codes vary by hospital.

cards.front: What does RACE stand for in a fire?
cards.back: Rescue anyone in immediate danger, Alarm by pulling the station and calling, Contain by closing doors and windows, and Extinguish or Evacuate. Evacuate horizontally first, then by stairs, never by elevator.

cards.front: What does PASS stand for?
cards.back: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the flames, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side. Only fight a small contained fire with a clear escape behind you.

cards.front: Why is oxygen a fire hazard, and when do you shut a zone valve?
cards.back: Oxygen does not burn but makes everything else burn faster and hotter, turning a harmless spark into a flash fire. Shut zone valves only on the order of the person running the response, since it cuts oxygen to every patient in that zone.

cards.front: What must NOT be done to a body in a medical examiner case?
cards.back: Do not remove tubes, lines, IOs, pads, dressings, or clothing. Do not wash the body or clean blood. Everything is potential evidence, and tube position may be a forensic question.

cards.front: Which deaths are typically reported to the medical examiner?
cards.back: Violent deaths including homicide, suicide, and accident, sudden or unexpected deaths, deaths in custody, suspected overdose, occupational deaths, procedure-related deaths, unattended deaths, and any suspicious or unexplained death.

cards.front: What is the rule on organ donation referral, and who talks to the family?
cards.back: Every death and imminent death is referred to the organ procurement organization, usually within about 1 hour, regardless of apparent candidacy. A trained requestor from that organization approaches the family, never ED staff.

cards.front: What is the evidence on family presence during resuscitation?
cards.back: It is supported when a staff member is assigned to stay with them and narrate in plain language. Families present report less anxiety and less complicated grief than those left waiting and imagining.

cards.front: What words do you use, and avoid, when telling a family someone has died?
cards.back: Use 'died' or 'dead' plainly and early. Avoid 'passed', 'lost', 'gone', 'didn't make it', 'I know how you feel', 'at least...', and 'she's in a better place'. Offer silence and concrete help.

cards.front: How do you prepare a family to view a body?
cards.back: Make the room presentable within medical examiner limits, dim lights, place a chair, and tell them beforehand what they will see including tubes, bruising, or injury. Offer to go in or wait outside, and do not rush.

cards.front: How are a deceased patient's belongings handled?
cards.back: Inventoried with a second staff member as witness and documented, valuables to the hospital safe with a receipt, and returned in a proper belongings bag, never a trash bag. Cut clothing is still theirs.

cards.front: What is the 'second victim' phenomenon?
cards.back: The clinician harmed by a bad patient outcome: intrusive replaying, self-doubt, anxiety, and avoidance, whether or not anything was done wrong. Debriefs, peer support, and employee assistance exist for it, and delayed reactions are normal.

quiz.q: You cared for a patient with C. difficile wearing gown and gloves. After doffing, what hand hygiene is required?
choices: Soap and water, because alcohol does not kill C. diff spores
Alcohol rub, which is preferred in all situations
None, because gloves were worn throughout
Alcohol rub followed by lotion
quiz.why: C. diff spores survive alcohol, so they must be physically removed by washing. Gloves leak and contaminate hands during removal, so gloving never substitutes for hand hygiene.

quiz.q: You enter a room, adjust the IV pole position, and leave without touching the patient. Which WHO moment applies?
