choices: None, since there was no patient contact
Moment 5, after touching patient surroundings
Moment 2, before a clean or aseptic procedure
Moment 3, after body fluid exposure risk
quiz.why: The patient's environment carries their organisms, so touching the surroundings requires hand hygiene on exit. Moment 2 applies before aseptic tasks and moment 3 after fluid exposure, neither of which occurred.

quiz.q: A new tech has gel manicure nails and asks whether that is allowed in the ED. What is correct?
choices: Allowed if kept short
Allowed if gloves are worn for all patient contact
Allowed only in non-clinical areas of the ED
Not allowed for staff with direct patient contact, because artificial nails harbor organisms and are linked to outbreaks
quiz.why: Artificial nails, gels, and wraps are prohibited for direct-care staff because organisms persist under and around them; outbreaks in newborn and intensive care units have been traced to them. Gloves and short length do not resolve the risk.

quiz.q: A patient with suspected measles arrives and you must place him. What is required?
choices: Surgical mask on staff and a private room with the door closed
Gown and gloves plus a private room
Fit-tested N95 on staff, negative-pressure room, door closed
Standard precautions only until the diagnosis is confirmed
quiz.why: Measles is airborne and requires an N95 or PAPR with a negative-pressure room. Surgical masks do not filter airborne particles, contact PPE addresses the wrong route, and waiting for confirmation exposes everyone in the interim.

quiz.q: A patient on droplet precautions for influenza must go to CT. What do you do?
choices: Place a surgical mask on the patient and notify CT of the precautions
Place an N95 on the patient
Cancel the study until precautions are lifted
Transport with no mask since the hallway is well ventilated
quiz.why: Source control means masking the patient with a surgical mask, and the receiving department must know so it can protect staff and clean afterward. An N95 on a patient is not indicated, and canceling necessary imaging is not the answer.

quiz.q: A disinfectant wipe label specifies a 4-minute contact time. The surface dries after about one minute. What must be done?
choices: Nothing; drying indicates the product has worked
Wipe with a second product to speed disinfection
Reapply the product so the surface remains visibly wet for the full 4 minutes
Let it dry and repeat in 4 minutes
quiz.why: Disinfectant efficacy is validated only for the labeled wet contact time, so a surface that dries early is not disinfected. Mixing products can neutralize them, and a dry interval does not count toward the contact time.

quiz.q: Which doffing sequence is correct?
choices: Mask, eye protection, gown, gloves, hand hygiene
Gloves, gown, hand hygiene, eye protection, mask, hand hygiene
Gown, mask, gloves, eye protection, hand hygiene
Eye protection, gloves, mask, gown, hand hygiene
quiz.why: The most contaminated items, gloves and gown, come off first while they still cover you, and the respirator comes off last because it protects you from the room's air. Removing a mask first exposes your airway inside a contaminated room.

quiz.q: You are donning PPE for a contact and droplet precautions room. In what order?
choices: Gloves, gown, mask, eye protection
Mask, gown, gloves, eye protection
Gown, gloves, mask, eye protection
Hand hygiene, gown, mask, eye protection, gloves
quiz.why: Hand hygiene starts the sequence, and gloves go on last so they cover the gown cuff and close the wrist gap. Any order that puts gloves before the gown leaves exposed skin at the wrist.

quiz.q: You put on an N95 for a TB rule-out patient. What must you do before entering?
choices: Perform a user seal check by covering the respirator and exhaling to feel for leaks
Repeat your annual fit test
Add a surgical mask over the N95 for extra protection
Nothing, because your fit test is current
quiz.why: A seal check is required every time a respirator is worn, because straps, positioning, and face shape on the day all affect the seal. Fit testing is a separate annual verification and does not replace the per-use check.

quiz.q: A tech is stuck by a used needle at the start of a 12-hour shift. The department is extremely busy. What is the correct action?
choices: Finish the shift and report to employee health in the morning
Wash and report immediately, because HIV prophylaxis is most effective within 2 hours
Report only if the source patient has known risk factors
Wash, squeeze out blood, and report at the end of the shift
quiz.why: Prophylaxis efficacy declines hourly and the outer limit is 72 hours, so immediate reporting is the clinical action, not paperwork. Source risk is determined by testing, not assumption, and milking the wound does not help.

quiz.q: Which statement about hepatitis exposures after a needlestick is correct?
choices: Hepatitis C has an effective post-exposure prophylaxis regimen
Hepatitis B requires no action regardless of vaccination status
Hepatitis B immune globulin plus vaccine is given to a non-immune worker, ideally within 24 hours
Neither hepatitis B nor C requires follow-up testing
quiz.why: There is no hepatitis C prophylaxis, only monitoring with early treatment if seroconversion occurs. Hepatitis B prophylaxis exists for the non-immune, and both require follow-up testing.

quiz.q: Which sharps practice is correct?
choices: Recap the needle with one hand before disposal
Hand the used needle to the nurse who will dispose of it
Set the needle on the tray table until you finish the task
Activate the safety device at the point of use and dispose of it yourself
quiz.why: The user disposes of their own sharp immediately after activating the safety device. Recapping causes a large share of sticks even one-handed, passing sharps transfers the risk, and a needle left on a surface reaches linen or another person.

quiz.q: You are about to draw blood. The patient's armband reads a date of birth of 03/07/1958 and the specimen label reads 03/07/1968. What do you do?
choices: Stop and resolve the mismatch with the nurse and registration before drawing anything
Draw and correct the label afterward
Ask the patient which is correct and draw
Draw, since the names match
quiz.why: Both identifiers must match exactly, because a mismatch can mean two different patients in the system and a mislabeled tube can cause a fatal transfusion or a wrong result acted on. Nothing is collected until it is resolved.

quiz.q: An elderly patient on the stretcher is confused and keeps trying to climb over the rail. You need to step out to get supplies. What is correct?
choices: Raise all four rails and step out briefly
Ask another staff member to stay with her before you leave
Put the bed alarm on and leave the door open
Tell her firmly to stay in bed and step out
quiz.why: A confused patient actively trying to get up is never left alone. Four rails constitute a restraint and an entrapment hazard, a bed alarm reports a fall rather than preventing it, and instructions do not work on a confused patient.

quiz.q: You notice that an IV was nearly started in a patient's arm bearing a pink band, and you spoke up in time. The patient was not harmed. What should happen?
choices: Nothing, since no harm occurred
Document in the patient's chart that a near miss occurred
File an incident report as a near miss, since it reveals a system flaw
Tell the nurse privately and let her decide
quiz.why: Near misses are free information about a flaw that will eventually reach a patient. The report is a safety document that stays out of the medical record, and the decision to report is not the nurse's alone.

quiz.q: An E cylinder reads 900 psi. The patient needs 10 L/min for a trip estimated at 30 minutes round trip. Is the tank sufficient?
choices: Yes, about 45 minutes
Yes, about 35 minutes
No, about 20 minutes, so get a full tank
Cannot be determined from these numbers
quiz.why: 900 minus 200 equals 700, times 0.28 equals 196, divided by 10 equals about 20 minutes, which does not cover a 30-minute trip plus reserve. The calculation is exactly why the formula is worth memorizing.

quiz.q: A patient who had a posterior hip replacement two days ago needs to move from bed to chair. What must be avoided?
choices: Using a gait belt
Bending the hip past 90 degrees, crossing the leg past midline, or rotating the leg inward
Placing the chair on the strong side
Locking the wheelchair wheels
quiz.why: Those three motions are what dislocate a posterior hip replacement. Gait belts, positioning on the strong side, and locking the wheels are all correct transfer practice and are not restricted.

quiz.q: A 260-pound patient who cannot bear weight needs to move from stretcher to bed. What is the correct approach?
choices: Two staff using a draw sheet and good body mechanics
One staff member using a gait belt
Ask the patient to scoot across with rail assistance
Use an air-assisted lateral transfer mat or mechanical lift with adequate staff and rated equipment
quiz.why: The safe manual lift limit for patient handling is about 35 pounds, so equipment is the answer rather than more people pulling harder. Draw sheets, gait belts, and self-scooting all exceed safe loading for a non-weight-bearing patient of this size.

quiz.q: A 15-year-old is placed in behavioral restraints. How long is the order valid before renewal?
choices: 1 hour
2 hours
4 hours
24 hours
quiz.why: Behavioral restraint orders are limited by age: 4 hours for adults 18 and over, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, and 1 hour for children under 9. A face-to-face evaluation is separately required within 1 hour of initiation.

quiz.q: A restrained, sedated patient is positioned prone with a staff member's weight on his upper back to complete the application. What is the danger?
choices: Positional asphyxia, a leading mechanism of restraint-associated death
Skin breakdown over the sternum
Loss of IV access
Impaired ability to document the restraint
quiz.why: Pressure on the back in a prone position prevents chest expansion and has killed patients. Supine with the head of the bed slightly elevated is standard, with continuous airway and vomiting surveillance.

quiz.q: What must be documented at each 15-minute check of a restrained patient?
choices: Only the presence of a pulse
The patient's stated reason for agitation
Circulation, skin integrity, range of motion, respiratory status, position, and offers of fluids and toileting
Only that the restraints remain secure
quiz.why: The checks exist to catch the harms restraint causes: ischemia, skin injury, contracture, airway compromise, and neglect of basic needs. Confirming security alone documents nothing about the patient's safety.

quiz.q: An intoxicated patient has been shouting for twenty minutes and refusing to sit. Nothing has been tried yet. What is the correct first step?
choices: Request an order for behavioral restraints
Reduce stimulation, address basic needs, and attempt verbal de-escalation
Have security place him in a safe room immediately
Ask the provider for a sedating medication
quiz.why: Least restrictive first is both a regulatory requirement and the most effective approach. Restraint and chemical sedation are the last rungs, and skipping to them without attempting de-escalation is both unsafe and indefensible in documentation.

quiz.q: You are interviewing a patient who stands up, clenches his fists, and steps toward the doorway you came in through. What is your priority?
choices: Continue the conversation to avoid escalating him
Sit down to appear less threatening
Reposition yourself for a clear exit, keep distance, and summon help
Tell him to sit down and calm himself
quiz.why: Losing your exit is the positioning failure that turns escalation into assault. Regaining a path to the door with distance maintained, plus early help, is the correct response. Sitting removes your ability to leave and commands escalate.

quiz.q: A small fire starts in a trash can in an empty hallway alcove. What is the correct order of action?
choices: Rescue anyone in danger, pull the alarm, close doors to contain, then extinguish if small with an exit behind you
Extinguish first since it is small, then pull the alarm
Evacuate all patients vertically by the nearest stairwell immediately
Shut all oxygen zone valves, then pull the alarm
quiz.why: RACE puts people first and the alarm before firefighting so help is already coming. Immediate vertical evacuation of an entire department is more dangerous than horizontal movement, and zone valves are closed only on command because they cut oxygen to every patient in the zone.

quiz.q: A code pink is announced overhead. What is a tech's role?
choices: Remain in your assigned zone and continue tasks
Report to the nursery
Cover assigned exits and stairwells and watch for anyone carrying a bag or bundle or leaving quickly
Call security for instructions
quiz.why: A code pink is an infant or child abduction, and every staff member becomes an observer at exits and stairwells. Continuing normal work defeats the response, and converging on the nursery leaves egress points uncovered.

quiz.q: A patient dies after a fall at home with a head injury. The family is waiting to view the body. What must you do first?
choices: Remove all lines and tubes and clean the patient before the family enters
Leave all lines, tubes, and clothing in place, because a fall death is a medical examiner case
Remove only the endotracheal tube for the family's comfort
Wash the body and dress it in a clean gown
quiz.why: A death from an accidental injury is reportable to the medical examiner, and tube position, wounds, and clothing may all be forensic evidence. You may straighten sheets and dim lights, but nothing is removed or washed.

quiz.q: Which statement about organ and tissue donation referral is correct?
choices: Referral is made only when the patient is a plausible organ donor
The ED nurse should ask the family for consent
Referral is unnecessary after cardiac death
Every death and imminent death is referred to the organ procurement organization, and a trained requestor approaches the family
quiz.why: Federal requirements call for timely referral of all deaths and imminent deaths regardless of apparent candidacy, and tissue and cornea donation remains possible after cardiac death. A trained requestor makes the approach, because how it is asked changes both consent and family distress.

quiz.q: A family has just been told their father died. The daughter asks you whether he was in pain. You were not in the room for the resuscitation. What is the best response?
choices: 'No, he didn't feel a thing'
'At least it was quick'
'I wasn't in the room, so I don't want to guess. Let me get the doctor who was with him so she can answer that.'
'I know how hard this is, I lost my father too'
quiz.why: Honesty plus a route to a real answer respects the question. Inventing reassurance risks being wrong about something that will matter forever, 'at least' minimizes the loss, and turning to your own story shifts the focus away from them.

quiz.q: Two weeks after a pediatric death you assisted with, a tech is replaying the case, avoiding the pediatric rooms, and sleeping poorly. What is this and what helps?
choices: Second victim response; debriefs, peer support, and the employee assistance program
A sign of unsuitability for emergency work; a transfer is indicated
Normal fatigue; nothing is needed
A performance problem requiring remediation
quiz.why: The second victim response is a recognized reaction in clinicians after a bad outcome, with delayed onset being common and unrelated to whether anything was done wrong. Structured support works; framing it as unsuitability or a performance issue prevents people from seeking help.

quiz.q: You are assigned to stay with a family during their father's resuscitation. What is your role?
choices: Explain the medications and their likely outcome
Keep them out of the room until it is over
Answer their clinical questions in detail so they are fully informed
Narrate in plain language what is happening, stay present, and take them out if they need to leave
quiz.why: The assigned support person provides presence and plain narration, not clinical interpretation or prognosis, which belong to the provider. Excluding the family removes a practice that evidence links to less anxiety and less complicated grief.

scenarios.title: The ladder, one rung at a time
scenarios.intro:
2140. Room 9 holds a man in his late twenties brought in by police after a bar fight. He is intoxicated, has a laceration above his right eyebrow, and is waiting for the provider. He has been here about ninety minutes.

You pass the door and see him pacing the length of the room, six steps each way, muttering. His hands open and close. The television is on loud, the overhead light is at full brightness, and two staff members are standing at the doorway watching him.

Nobody has done anything yet.

steps.prompt: Rung one of the ladder. What is the first intervention?

choices.text: Reduce the stimulation: turn down or off the television, lower the lights, and clear the audience from the doorway
choices.feedback: Correct, and it costs nothing. An audience of staff watching an agitated man is fuel, and sensory load drives agitation in an intoxicated patient.

choices.text: Call security to post at the door now
choices.feedback: Show of presence is rung four. Jumping there first escalates a situation that environmental changes often resolve, and it is harder to step back down the ladder than up it.

choices.text: Tell him to sit down and stop pacing
choices.feedback: A command with no relationship behind it and no offer attached. This reliably escalates, and it hands him a confrontation he is looking for.

choices.text: Close the door and leave him alone until the provider is free
choices.feedback: Ignoring an escalating intoxicated patient with a head laceration is both a safety and a clinical failure. He may also be deteriorating from a head injury.

steps.prompt: Television off, lights down, doorway cleared. He is still pacing but glances at you. You go to rung two: basic needs. What do you actually ask about?

choices.text: Whether he is hungry, cold, in pain, needs the bathroom, or wants to call someone
choices.feedback: This is the rung people skip and it resolves an enormous share of agitation. Hunger, cold, a full bladder, pain, and nicotine withdrawal are the usual engines.

choices.text: Whether he is going to cooperate with the staff
choices.feedback: That is a demand dressed as a question. It offers him nothing and invites a no.

choices.text: Whether he has been drinking and how much
choices.feedback: A clinically relevant question, but asked now it reads as an accusation and it is not what this rung is for. The nurse and provider will ask it.

choices.text: Whether he wants something for the pain
choices.feedback: Pain is a legitimate part of basic needs and asking is fine. Just be careful not to imply you can provide medication, which you cannot. Report it to the nurse.

steps.prompt: He says, 'Nobody has told me anything in two hours and my head is killing me and I want to go outside and smoke.' He is loud but he is talking to you. Rung three, verbal de-escalation. What do you say?

choices.text: 'You've been sitting here two hours with a cut on your head and nobody has updated you. That would make me angry too. I'm going to get your nurse right now, and I'll bring you a blanket and some water while you wait.'
choices.feedback: This is the move: something true about his situation, said plainly, plus one concrete thing you will actually do. Acknowledgment without action is hollow; action without acknowledgment is a transaction.

choices.text: 'You can't smoke here. I'll see if the nurse can come by at some point.'
choices.feedback: A refusal and a vague promise. You answered the least important part of what he said and ignored the two-hour wait and the pain.

choices.text: 'I understand. Calm down and I'll see what I can do.'
choices.feedback: 'Calm down' is a command that has never calmed anyone, and 'see what I can do' commits to nothing he can rely on.

choices.text: 'I hear you. Would you rather sit in the chair or on the bed while I go get your nurse?'
choices.feedback: Offering a real choice restores a sense of control and is good technique. Pair it with the honest acknowledgment of the wait and it would be complete.

steps.prompt: You come back with a blanket and the nurse. As she starts to explain the plan, he throws the blanket, steps toward her, and says, 'I'll put you through that wall.' He is between her and the door.

choices.text: Position to keep both of you a path to the exit, keep two arm lengths, call for security and additional staff immediately
choices.feedback: Correct. A direct threat with a closed exit is the end of verbal de-escalation for now. Distance, exit, and help, in that order, and nobody is required to stay in that room.

choices.text: Step between the nurse and the patient to shield her
choices.feedback: Brave and wrong. Closing distance with a threatening person creates the assault you are trying to prevent. Create space and get help.

choices.text: Keep talking calmly and continue trying to de-escalate from where you are
choices.feedback: De-escalation is right up to a direct threat with your exit blocked. Past that point, the priority is space and staff.

choices.text: Try to reach past him to hit the panic button on the far wall
choices.feedback: Reaching past a threatening person invites contact. Know where the panic buttons are before you need them, and use the one you can reach without crossing him, or call out.

steps.prompt: Security arrives, he swings at an officer, and the provider orders behavioral restraints. He is 27 years old. The team applies four-point restraints supine with the head of the bed slightly elevated, and you are assigned the monitoring.

choices.text: Checks at least every 15 minutes documenting circulation, skin, range of motion, breathing, and position, with offers of fluids and toileting, and confirm the face-to-face evaluation happens within 1 hour and the order is renewed at 4 hours
choices.feedback: All of it. The 4-hour adult limit, the 1-hour face-to-face, and the 15-minute checks are federal requirements, not local preference, and the checks are where restraint harm actually gets caught.

choices.text: Check on him hourly since he is sedated and quiet now
choices.feedback: The quiet twenty minutes after application is the most dangerous window. Aspiration, positional compromise, and circulation loss all happen while everyone assumes someone else is watching.

choices.text: Tie the wrist restraints to the side rails so they are easier to reach
choices.feedback: Never to the rails. Dropping a rail with a limb tied to it wrenches the joint. Tie to the bed frame on the part that moves with the bed, with quick-release knots.

choices.text: Do the 15-minute checks and also stay continuously present as the 1:1 observer
choices.feedback: Correct, and continuous observation is standard for behavioral restraint. Just make sure the documented checks actually happen on the clock and are not replaced by 'I was in the room.'

scenarios.debrief:
The ladder exists because each rung resolves a real percentage of cases, and skipping rungs is both less effective and indefensible afterward.

Rung one cost nothing: a television, a light switch, and moving three people out of a doorway. Rung two was a sandwich-and-blanket question, which resolves more agitation than any medication. Rung three was one true sentence about his situation plus one concrete action, which is the highest-yield sentence in de-escalation.

What ended the verbal phase was not the yelling, it was the direct threat with the exit blocked. At that point the rules change to distance, exit, and help, and stepping between people is bravery that produces injuries.

The restraint numbers are not negotiable and you should be able to say them cold: an adult order lasts `4 hours`, `2 hours` for ages 9 to 17, `1 hour` under 9. A face-to-face evaluation within `1 hour` of initiation. Checks at least every `15 minutes` covering circulation, skin, range of motion, breathing, position, and offers of fluids and toileting. Supine, never prone with weight on the back. Tied to the frame, never the rails. Quick-release knots. And the most dangerous moment is the quiet one right after, when the room clears and everyone assumes someone else is watching.

scenarios.title: Chair 11, three weeks of cough
scenarios.intro:
1520 on a Thursday. The waiting room has fourteen people. You are doing scheduled reassessments.

Chair 11 is a 41-year-old man, thin, wearing a jacket in a warm room. He has been coughing for the twenty minutes you have been out here, a deep productive cough, and he keeps wiping his mouth with a tissue. His triage note reads: cough, ESI 4.

When you take his vitals he tells you the cough has been going on for about three weeks, he wakes up soaked in sweat most nights, and he has lost 'maybe fifteen, twenty pounds' without trying. He recently moved here and stayed in a shelter for two months.

steps.prompt: You have four pieces of information: cough over three weeks, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, and congregate living. What does this pattern suggest and what do you do first?

choices.text: Recognize possible tuberculosis and immediately place a surgical mask on the patient, then move him out of the general waiting area
choices.feedback: Correct, and the order matters. Source control first, because every cough in that lobby is an exposure to fourteen people while you go find someone.

choices.text: Finish the rest of your reassessments, then report the history to the nurse
choices.feedback: That is several more minutes of an unmasked, coughing possible TB patient sitting among fourteen people including anyone immunocompromised.

choices.text: Put on an N95 yourself and continue taking his vitals in the lobby
choices.feedback: Protecting yourself is reasonable but incomplete. The mask that matters most right now is the one on the patient, because it stops the aerosol at the source.

choices.text: Tell the nurse he has a bad cough and let her decide
choices.feedback: You buried the finding. It is not 'a bad cough', it is three weeks plus night sweats plus weight loss plus congregate living, which is a classic TB presentation.

steps.prompt: He is masked and you have walked him to a side corridor away from the other patients. What do you tell the charge nurse?

choices.text: 'Chair 11, 41-year-old male, triaged ESI 4 for cough. Three weeks of productive cough, night sweats, about 20 pounds unintentional weight loss, two months in a shelter. Temp 37.9, respirations 20. I've masked him and moved him out of the lobby. I think he needs airborne isolation.'
choices.feedback: Complete and actionable: who, the risk factors in a line, what you already did, and what you think is needed. She can call for the negative-pressure room without asking you anything.

choices.text: 'I think chair 11 has TB.'
choices.feedback: It will get attention, but stating a diagnosis rather than the findings is out of your lane and gives her nothing to act on. Give her the four risk factors and let the conclusion be obvious.

choices.text: 'Chair 11 has been coughing a lot and should probably come back sooner.'
choices.feedback: You have lost the entire signal. Night sweats, weight loss, duration, and congregate living are the information; 'coughing a lot' is not.

choices.text: 'Chair 11 needs a negative-pressure room, can you get one?'
choices.feedback: The right destination, but with no reasoning attached. A charge nurse juggling twenty things needs the why in the same sentence as the ask.

steps.prompt: A negative-pressure room is available. You are going to room him and stay to get a full set of vitals and set up for a chest X-ray order. What PPE do you put on, and in what order?

choices.text: Hand hygiene, gown, fit-tested N95 with a seal check, eye protection, gloves over the gown cuff
choices.feedback: Correct sequence, and the seal check is the step people skip. Airborne precautions technically require the respirator and the room; gown and gloves are added by many hospitals and by the tasks you are doing.

choices.text: Hand hygiene, gloves, surgical mask, gown
choices.feedback: Two errors. A surgical mask does not filter airborne particles, and gloves before the gown leaves your wrists exposed.

choices.text: Hand hygiene and a fit-tested N95 only, since TB is airborne and not contact
choices.feedback: Defensible on pure transmission grounds, and some hospitals do exactly this. But follow your posted sign, and for hands-on tasks with a coughing patient, gown, eyes, and gloves are the safer default.

choices.text: N95 first, then hand hygiene, then gown, gloves, eye protection
choices.feedback: Hand hygiene starts the sequence, and eye protection goes on before gloves. The N95 is right; the order is not.

steps.prompt: You are in the room. A colleague pushes the door partly open from the hallway, without a respirator, to ask you a quick question. What do you do?

choices.text: Tell her to close the door, and step out to talk to her after you doff, because an open door defeats the negative pressure
choices.feedback: Exactly. Negative pressure requires a sealed room, and an open door puts infectious aerosol into the corridor and exposes her without a respirator.

choices.text: Answer quickly since the conversation will take ten seconds
choices.feedback: Ten seconds of an open negative-pressure room with a coughing TB patient is a real exposure to her and to the hallway.

choices.text: Hand her an N95 through the doorway and continue the conversation
choices.feedback: An untested, unsealed respirator handed to someone in a doorway is not protection, and the door is still open.

choices.text: Gesture for her to close the door and hold up a hand to indicate you will come out
choices.feedback: Fine, as long as the door actually closes immediately and you do not carry on a conversation through a gap.

steps.prompt: The workup is underway and you are leaving the room. Where do you doff each item?

choices.text: Gloves and gown inside the room, hand hygiene, then eye protection and the N95 after you exit with the door closed, then hand hygiene again
choices.feedback: Correct. The respirator is the last thing protecting you from the room's air, so it comes off after you are out and the door is shut.

choices.text: Remove the N95 first so you can breathe more easily, then gown and gloves
choices.feedback: This exposes your airway while still inside an airborne isolation room with a coughing patient. The respirator is always last.

choices.text: Everything in the room, including the N95, then hand hygiene outside
choices.feedback: Gloves and gown inside is right, but taking off the respirator inside the room defeats its purpose in the final seconds.

choices.text: Everything outside the room in the corridor so nothing is left inside
choices.feedback: The opposite problem. Walking a contaminated gown and gloves into the hallway spreads what you just contained.

scenarios.debrief:
The whole case turned on recognizing a pattern from four pieces of history, none of which was in the triage note.

The classic tuberculosis picture: **cough lasting more than 2 to 3 weeks**, **night sweats**, **unintentional weight loss**, often with fever or blood-streaked sputum, in someone with a risk factor such as congregate living, incarceration, homelessness, HIV, or birth in a high-prevalence country. An ESI 4 triage note for 'cough' is not wrong; it is just incomplete, and you were the person who happened to ask.

The sequence is worth memorizing because you will use it for TB, measles, and chickenpox alike: **mask the patient first**, because source control stops the aerosol where it starts. **Move them out of the shared space.** **Report the findings, not a diagnosis**, in one structured sentence with the risk factors named. **Negative-pressure room, door closed.** **Fit-tested N95 with a seal check on you**, never a surgical mask. **Doff gloves and gown inside, respirator outside.**

And the last detail is the one that actually fails in practice: the door. Negative pressure is not a property of the room, it is a property of the room being closed. Every conversation held through a propped door undoes all of it.
